question.prompt: Let \(T\) be the triangle in the coordinate plane with vertices \((0,0),\) \((4,0),\) and \((0,3).\) Consider the following five isometries (rigid transformations) of the plane: rotations of \(90^{\circ},\) \(180^{\circ},\) and \(270^{\circ}\) counterclockwise around the origin, reflection across the \(x\)-axis, and reflection across the \(y\)-axis. How many of the \(125\) sequences of three of these transformations (not necessarily distinct) will return \(T\) to its original position? (For example, a \(180^{\circ}\) rotation, followed by a reflection across the \(x\)-axis, followed by a reflection across the \(y\)-axis will return \(T\) to its original position, but a \(90^{\circ}\) rotation, followed by a reflection across the \(x\)-axis, followed by another reflection across the \(x\)-axis will not return \(T\) to its original position.)

solutions.title: Count rotations and reflections
solutions.explanation:
The two nonzero vertices have different distances from the origin, so returning the triangle requires returning each vertex individually. This lets us count sequences whose combined transformation is the identity, meaning that every point returns to itself.

Write \(O=(0,0)\), \(A=(4,0)\), and \(B=(0,3)\). Every allowed move fixes \(O\) and preserves distances from it, so a returned triangle must fix both \(A\) and \(B\). A rigid motion fixing three noncollinear points is the identity: any point is determined by its distances to those three points.

Rotations preserve the counterclockwise order of the labeled vertices \(O,A,B\), while a reflection reverses it. Thus a successful sequence must contain an even number of reflections, either zero or two.

If there are zero reflections, measure each rotation in quarter-turns. The three numbers belong to \(\{1,2,3\}\), and their sum must be a multiple of \(4\). Their sum lies between \(3\) and \(9\), so it must be \(4\) or \(8\). The only possibilities, ignoring order, are
\[
(1,1,2)\qquad\text{and}\qquad(2,3,3).
\]
Each has three orders, determined by the position of the number appearing once. This gives \(6\) sequences.

If there are two reflections, there is one rotation. A \(90^\circ\) or \(270^\circ\) rotation exchanges the coordinate axes, whereas each axis reflection leaves both coordinate axes in place as sets. Such a sequence would send \(A\) to the \(y\)-axis, so the rotation must be \(180^\circ\).

A half-turn changes both coordinate signs. To undo those changes, the reflections must change the \(x\)-sign once and the \(y\)-sign once. Therefore we need one reflection across each axis. These three moves only change signs, so every order works. Since the moves are distinct, there are \(3\cdot2\cdot1=6\) orders.

The cases are disjoint and exhaustive, giving
\[
6+6=\boxed{12},
\]
choice \(\mathrm{A}\).

solutions.title: Let the last move be forced
solutions.explanation:
Once the first two moves are chosen, there is exactly one transformation that undoes their combined effect. We can therefore count suitable ordered pairs instead of examining all \(125\) triples.

Every move fixes the origin and preserves distances. Since the other vertices have distances \(4\) and \(3\) from the origin, a sequence returning the triangle must fix those vertices individually. A rigid motion fixing three noncollinear points is the identity, because every point is determined by its distances to those three points.

Each of the five allowed moves has an allowed inverse: the \(90^\circ\) and \(270^\circ\) rotations undo each other, and the other three moves undo themselves. Thus the first two moves can be completed successfully exactly when their combined effect is one of the five allowed moves.

There are three types of ordered pairs.

1. Two rotations. There are \(3\cdot3=9\) pairs. Exactly three already give the identity:
\[
(90^\circ,270^\circ),\quad(180^\circ,180^\circ),\quad(270^\circ,90^\circ).
\]
These would require an unavailable \(0^\circ\) rotation as the third move. Each of the remaining \(9-3=6\) pairs gives a nonidentity allowed rotation.

2. One rotation and one reflection. A half-turn combined with one axis reflection gives the other axis reflection, since the half-turn changes both signs and the reflection changes one sign. There are two choices of reflection and two orders, giving \(4\) pairs. A quarter-turn combined with an axis reflection instead has coordinate rule \((x,y)\mapsto(y,x)\) or \((x,y)\mapsto(-y,-x)\). These are diagonal reflections, neither of which is allowed, so they give no additional pairs.

3. Two reflections. Repeating the same reflection gives the identity and cannot work. Using the two different axis reflections changes both signs, giving a half-turn. The two possible orders both work, giving \(2\) pairs.

Every counted pair has exactly one successful third move, and different ordered pairs produce different sequences. Therefore the answer is
\[
6+4+2=\boxed{12},
\]
choice \(\mathrm{A}\).
